lines.text: Instructor / source: Corey Schafer - Python Tutorial: CSV Module - How to Read, Parse, and
Write CSV Files Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q5uM4VKywbA Assigned use:
OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range; CSV/DictReader context only.
Book + lab required.
A CSV file looks simple enough to tempt beginners into treating it as ordinary text. That is
dangerous. A comma can be data inside a quoted field; a newline can be represented differently
across systems; an ID such as 0007 can lose meaning if something guesses it is a number. In
the supplied module file, the first product is Notebook, A5. A naive line.split(",") would
invent an extra column and silently shift the row.
Picture the raw file as evidence arriving at a receiving desk. Your first job is not to make it
pretty. Your first job is to know exactly what arrived and to parse it according to the file format.
Python's csv module understands quoting rules that a manual split does not. csv.DictReader
also gives each parsed value a column name, which makes later validation readable.
Before transforming anything, record the source path, bytes or checksum when practical,
header names and raw record count. A parser accepting the file does not prove the schema is
the one your pipeline expected. order_id,customer_id,... and customer,order,... are both
syntactically valid CSV headers; only one matches your contract.
Follow the source file once with csv.DictReader. Print only a small bounded sample, the field
names and row count. Confirm that Notebook, A5 remains one product value. Then calculate a
SHA-256 checksum of the source file without rewriting it. That checksum is a fingerprint of the
exact bytes, not a statement that the data is correct.
A common beginner mistake is to open the raw CSV in a spreadsheet, fix a cell manually, save
it, and then run the pipeline. That destroys the distinction between source and transformation.
Another is to let a library infer an ID column as numeric and later wonder where leading zeros
went. Raw preservation and explicit typing prevent these problems from becoming invisible.
Follow with me once
Start by proving that a CSV parser understands a quoted comma and that the source file
remains untouched.
from pathlib import Path
import csv, hashlib
source = Path("data/M05_Module_Orders.csv")
raw_bytes = source.read_bytes()
checksum = hashlib.sha256(raw_bytes).hexdigest()
with source.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
reader = csv.DictReader(f)
rows = list(reader)
print(reader.fieldnames)
print("rows=", len(rows))
print("first_product=", rows[0]["product"])
print("sha256=", checksum)
Predict before running: there are 9 raw records and the first product must be exactly Notebook,
A5, not two fields. If split(",") had been used, the first line would appear to have an extra
value and the column alignment would be wrong.
The checksum proves which bytes you processed; it does not prove those bytes are good data.
Keep those ideas separate: identity of input and quality of input are different controls.
Now inspect only bounded evidence:
required = {"order_id", "customer_id", "order_date", "quantity", "unit_price", "region", \
"product"}
missing = required - set(reader.fieldnames or [])
print("missing_required_columns=", sorted(missing))
print("sample_ids=", [r["order_id"] for r in rows[:3]])
Expected: no required columns are missing and the first three IDs are MO01, MO02, MO03. This is a
schema check, not yet a record-validity check. Later lessons decide whether each row is
acceptable.
Your independent practice
Parse M05_Module_Orders.csv with csv.DictReader. Record header, raw row count and
checksum. Prove the quoted product containing a comma remains one field. Then explain why
split(",") is not a CSV parser.
Changed retry - only after review
Create a new CSV with a quoted city value Delhi, NCR and an ID 0009. Parse it without losing
field boundaries or leading-zero identity.
Ready-made revision
Reconstruct the core contract of CSV properly: parse, inspect, preserve raw from memory. State
the input grain/state, one failure mode, one independent validation, and what evidence you
would keep. Then do one fresh 10-20 minute micro-task without video, review or AI solving
open.
Evidence to keep
Save code/config used, observed output or error, one independent validation, one own-words
explanation, and any repair/retry as a separate artifact. Do not overwrite the first attempt.
Instructor / source: Corey Schafer - Python Tutorial: Working with JSON Data using the json
Module Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9N6a-VLBa2I Assigned use:
OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range; JSON context only. Book + lab required.
JSON is not "a dictionary file." JSON is a serialization format that can hold objects, arrays, strings,
numbers, booleans and null values. A JSON document can contain one nested object whose
orders field is an array. JSON Lines (JSONL/NDJSON) instead stores one complete JSON value per
line, which is convenient for streams and append-style event files. Treating the two as
interchangeable leads to broken parsers and wrong record counts.
Open M05_Nested_Orders.json. The top level represents one batch document, not one order.
The actual order grain is inside the orders array. One order has a nested customer object, one
has an empty lines array, and one has customer: null. Those cases have different meanings.
An empty list means the list is known and currently has no elements; null means the customer
value itself is absent/unknown under this fixture.
Now inspect M05_Order_Events.jsonl. Each nonblank line is one event. You can process it line
by line and report the line number if one record is malformed, instead of making the entire file
an all-or-nothing mystery. Preserve the original line or source position in rejection evidence
when possible.
When flattening nested JSON, do not casually duplicate header-level measures across child
arrays and then sum them. You already saw that fan-out problem in SQL. The same grain logic
applies in Python. If one order has three line objects, expanding the lines makes three rows. An
order-level fee copied onto those rows is safe to display but unsafe to sum three times.
Your independent proof for this lesson should state three grains explicitly: the batch document
grain, the orders array grain, and the JSONL event grain. Then change the input with one order
whose customer object gains a new optional field. Decide whether that is compatible with your
parser instead of silently dropping or assuming the field.
Follow with me once
Read the nested JSON as one document, then deliberately move to the actual order array grain.
from pathlib import Path
import json
batch = json.loads(Path("data/M05_Nested_Orders.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
print("batch_id=", batch["batch_id"])
print("orders=", len(batch["orders"]))
for order in batch["orders"]:
customer = order.get("customer")
customer_id = None if customer is None else customer.get("id")
print(order["order_id"], "customer=", customer_id, "line_count=", len(order["lines"]))
You should see one batch document containing 3 orders. J102 has an empty lines list, while
J103 has customer = None. Those are not the same condition: one says a known collection has
zero members; the other says a value is absent.
Now treat JSONL differently:
path = Path("data/M05_Order_Events.jsonl")
events = []
with path.open(encoding="utf-8") as f:
for line_no, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
if not line.strip():
continue
event = json.loads(line)
event["source_line"] = line_no
events.append(event)
print("events=", len(events))
print("event_ids=", [e["event_id"] for e in events])
Expected: 3 events, with source lines preserved. If line 2 later becomes malformed, the
rejection can say exactly which source record failed instead of only saying "the JSON file is bad."
Your independent practice
Read the nested JSON and JSONL fixtures. State the grain of the batch, order array and event
lines. Count each correctly and preserve a source locator for one missing customer case.
Changed retry - only after review
Create a three-line JSONL file where the second event has an optional nested metadata object.
Process each line and explain compatibility without forcing all events to identical shape.
Ready-made revision
Reconstruct the core contract of JSON and JSONL from zero from memory. State the input
grain/state, one failure mode, one independent validation, and what evidence you would keep.
Then do one fresh 10-20 minute micro-task without video, review or AI solving open.

explanation, and any repair/retry as a separate artifact. Do not overwrite the first attempt.
Instructor / source: Corey Schafer - Python Tutorial: Pathlib - The Modern Way to Handle File
Paths Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yxa-DJuuTBI Assigned use:
OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range; Pathlib context only. Book + lab required.
A reliable data script must not depend on whatever folder happened to be open in the terminal.
Path("data/file.csv") is resolved relative to the current working directory, which can change
depending on how the script is launched. Path(__file__).resolve() gives you a stable anchor
to the script file itself. The difference becomes important as soon as automation runs your code
from a scheduler or another directory.
Picture a small landing zone with four shelves: incoming, raw, processed, and rejected. Files
should move through that lifecycle by explicit rules. Do not select "the first CSV" from an
unordered directory listing and hope it is today's file. Sort deterministic file lists or, better, select
by a declared manifest/business date.
A deterministic batch means the same declared inputs are discovered in the same order and
produce the same logical result. Determinism is not the same as idempotency: deterministic
code can still append duplicates every time it reruns. We will return to safe reruns later.
Use Path.glob() or rglob() deliberately, convert the result to a sorted list if order matters,
and log only safe metadata: filename, size, checksum, business date, record count. If a
destination filename already exists, do not overwrite it automatically unless your contract
explicitly says that the same content is being replaced. A checksum mismatch under the same
source name is a data-lineage event worth surfacing.
The changed retry is deliberately different: process three files whose lexical filename order
differs from their business-date order. Make the selection rule explicit and prove which order
your program follows.
Follow with me once
Anchor paths to the script, discover files deterministically, and write a manifest instead of
trusting whatever directory the terminal happens to be in.
from pathlib import Path
import hashlib, json
HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
landing = HERE / "incoming"
files = sorted(landing.glob("*.csv"))
manifest = []
for path in files:
raw = path.read_bytes()
manifest.append({
"name": path.name,
"bytes": len(raw),
"sha256": hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest(),
(HERE / "evidence").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(HERE / "evidence" / "manifest.json").write_text(
json.dumps(manifest, indent=2), encoding="utf-8"
Run the same script from two different working directories. If the script is correctly anchored, it
discovers the same declared landing folder both times. That is the point of separating script
location from current working directory.
A sorted file list is deterministic only with respect to the chosen sort key. If business order
should be based on a date inside each file rather than filename, read that date and sort by the
business key explicitly. "Sorted" is not automatically the same as "correct order."
Your independent practice
Create incoming/raw/processed/rejected folders in your own workspace. Discover three small
files deterministically and write a manifest with filename, bytes and checksum without
modifying source files.
Changed retry - only after review
Use filenames whose lexical order conflicts with a business_date inside each file. Implement and
explain the intended ordering rule.
Ready-made revision
Reconstruct the core contract of Paths, folders and deterministic batch files from memory. State
the input grain/state, one failure mode, one independent validation, and what evidence you
would keep. Then do one fresh 10-20 minute micro-task without video, review or AI solving
open.

Instructor / source: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics Link:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wUSDVGivd-8 Assigned use: 4:22:56-5:08:26 - pandas
intro, inspection, cleaning and analysis. Stop before copying an answer.
Profiling means looking before changing. In a production incident, the most expensive cleaning
mistake is often a transformation applied before anyone recorded what was wrong with the
source. Load the module CSV into pandas and first inspect shape, columns, dtypes, null counts,
key uniqueness and a bounded sample. Do not begin with fillna(0) or drop_duplicates()
merely because those commands exist.
The DataFrame has a grain just like a SQL table. Here one raw row is one delivered order record
from the training file, including records that may later be rejected. The raw DataFrame therefore
has nine rows. After cleaning, your accepted dataset will have a different population; comparing
statistics without naming the population is misleading.
Use df.shape, df.columns, df.dtypes, df.isna().sum(), and targeted nunique/duplicated
checks. describe() is useful for numeric distributions only after you understand whether a
column was parsed as numeric and whether invalid strings forced it to object/string. A column
with oops in unit_price should make you investigate, not automatically coerce everything to
zero.
Profiling outputs should be small enough to reason about. Dumping thousands of rows to the
terminal is not inspection. Save a compact profile: raw row count, key duplicate count, missing
counts for critical fields, parse-failure counts, and a few representative records.
In the independent task, profile the fresh inventory file without cleaning it. Predict which
columns should be numeric/date/key fields, then compare that contract with what pandas
inferred. Explain at least one reason inference is not business validation.
Follow with me once
Profile before transforming. The goal is to create a compact source-state report that you can
compare with later stages.
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("data/M05_Module_Orders.csv", dtype={"order_id": "string", "customer_id": \
"string"})
print("shape=", df.shape)
print("columns=", list(df.columns))
print("dtypes=", df.dtypes.astype(str).to_dict())
print("nulls=", df.isna().sum().to_dict())
print("duplicate_order_ids=", int(df["order_id"].duplicated(keep=False).sum()))
Expected raw shape is (9, 7). The two occurrences of MO02 should be visible as a duplicate-key
risk. A blank customer_id should remain evidence of missing identity rather than being silently
replaced.
Notice that pandas may infer a surprising dtype when one invalid string such as oops appears in
unit_price. That is not pandas being "wrong"; it is evidence that the source column is not
uniformly parseable as a number. Your next step is a deliberate parser/validator, not a blanket
fillna(0) or forced cast that hides the bad value.
Your independent practice
Profile M05_Fresh_Inventory.csv before cleaning: shape, columns, inferred dtypes, missing
values, duplicate SKU count and suspected parse failures. Save the profile separately from
source.
Changed retry - only after review
Profile a changed file containing a blank numeric field and one duplicate key; do not clean it.
Produce only observations and suspected risks.
Ready-made revision

input grain/state, one failure mode, one independent validation, and what evidence you would
keep. Then do one fresh 10-20 minute micro-task without video, review or AI solving open.

Instructor / source: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics Link:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wUSDVGivd-8 Assigned use: 4:22:56-5:08:26 - pandas
mechanics refresher; course rejected-row design is deeper than the video.
Cleaning is a controlled transformation, not a command to "make the file work." The safest
beginner pattern is to keep the raw records intact, derive parsed/cleaned values separately, and
split records into accepted and rejected outputs with explicit reason codes. Rejected data is not
trash; it is evidence about what the pipeline could not safely interpret or accept.
For the module practical, an order needs a nonblank customer ID, a unique order ID within the
batch, a valid ISO date, a positive integer quantity and a valid nonnegative unit price. Notice
how these are different kinds of checks: missing identity, batch-level uniqueness, parse validity
and business-range validity. One record may fail more than one rule, so preserve all relevant
reasons where practical.
Do not turn oops into zero. Zero is a valid business number with a meaning; oops is a parse
failure. Do not turn a missing customer into UNKNOWN unless the downstream contract explicitly
authorizes an unknown member and you preserve the provenance. These shortcuts make a
pipeline "complete" by inventing facts.
The supplied validator deliberately marks both occurrences of duplicated MO02 as rejected. That
policy is conservative: the batch does not tell us which of the two is authoritative. Keeping the
first and deleting the second would be an assumption. Another valid system might resolve
duplicates using source timestamps or version numbers, but those fields do not exist here.
Your validation contract must end with arithmetic: raw = accepted + rejected; accepted keys
are unique; every rejected row has at least one reason; accepted amount can be recomputed
from accepted quantity and price. Later systems will add stronger reconciliation, but this habit
starts now.
Follow with me once
Use the supplied validator as a readable example of accepted/rejected separation. Do not
mutate the raw rows to make them pass.
import csv
from M05_Validation import validate_orders
with open("data/M05_Module_Orders.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
raw = list(csv.DictReader(f))
accepted, rejected = validate_orders(raw)
print("raw=", len(raw), "accepted=", len(accepted), "rejected=", len(rejected))
print("accepted_ids=", [r["order_id"] for r in accepted])
print("rejected=", [(r.get("order_id"), r["rejection_reasons"]) for r in rejected])
For the supplied fixture the independent controls are 9 raw = 4 accepted + 5 rejected.
Accepted IDs are MO01, MO05, MO06, MO07. Both MO02 records are rejected because the batch
does not tell us which duplicate is authoritative. MO09 is rejected because unit_price='oops' is
not a price; it is not converted to zero.
Then reconcile money only over accepted rows:
accepted_amount = sum(float(r["amount"]) for r in accepted)
assert len(raw) == len(accepted) + len(rejected)
assert len({r["order_id"] for r in accepted}) == len(accepted)
print("accepted_amount=", accepted_amount)
Expected accepted amount is 5100.0. A clean-looking output without these row/key/amount
controls is weaker evidence than a visibly rejected bad row plus reconciliation.
Your independent practice
Validate the module orders into accepted/rejected outputs with explicit reasons. Do not read the
review controls first. Reconcile raw = accepted + rejected and prove accepted IDs unique.
Changed retry - only after review
Use the fresh inventory fixture: valid unique SKU, positive integer quantity, nonnegative decimal
cost and ISO received date. Split accepted/rejected with reasons.

Instructor / source: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics Link:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wUSDVGivd-8 Assigned use:
OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range; pandas merge context only.
A pandas merge is a join, so every SQL cardinality lesson still applies. If orders are many-to-one
with customers, the customer key must be unique on the right side. merge(...,
validate="many_to_one") can convert that assumption into an executable check instead of a
comment. The indicator=True option can also show which rows were matched or left
unmatched.
Start with the accepted order records, not the raw rejected population. Then load
M05_Customers.csv and prove customer_id is unique before the merge. Record order row
count and accepted amount before joining. Perform a left merge with
validate="many_to_one"; after the merge, the order row count and accepted amount must
remain unchanged. Customer attributes may be added, but one order must not become two.
Next deliberately substitute M05_Customers_Duplicate_Key.csv. The correct behavior is not to
celebrate that pandas produced more rows. With validate="many_to_one", pandas should
raise a MergeError because the right-side key is no longer unique. That is a desirable failure: the
program caught a broken relationship before money was multiplied.
Pandas has an important difference from ordinary SQL: merge documentation warns that null
keys on both sides may match each other. Do not assume SQL null join semantics carry over
unchanged. Critical join keys should have a deliberate missing-key policy before the merge.
For independent practice, aggregate accepted order amount by customer segment after a
validated merge and prove the group totals reconcile to the pre-merge accepted amount. Then
explain why a matching grand total alone would still not prove that each order was assigned to
the right customer.
Follow with me once
Turn your relationship assumption into executable code before aggregating.
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame([
{"order_id":"MO01", "customer_id":"C01", "amount":1000.0},
{"order_id":"MO05", "customer_id":"C04", "amount":1600.0},
{"order_id":"MO06", "customer_id":"C05", "amount":1500.0},
{"order_id":"MO07", "customer_id":"C01", "amount":1000.0},
customers = pd.read_csv("data/M05_Customers.csv")
before_rows = len(orders)
before_amount = orders["amount"].sum()
merged = orders.merge(
customers,
on="customer_id",
how="left",
validate="many_to_one",
indicator=True,
assert len(merged) == before_rows
assert merged["amount"].sum() == before_amount
print(merged.groupby("segment", dropna=False)["amount"].sum())
The merge is allowed to add customer attributes, but it is not allowed to multiply orders or
money. validate="many_to_one" makes the right-side uniqueness contract executable.
Now substitute M05_Customers_Duplicate_Key.csv. The desired result is a MergeError, not a
larger table. A controlled failure is stronger than a silent fan-out. After a valid merge, group
totals should reconcile back to 5100.0. The grand total alone is not enough, however; you must
also prove row preservation and key relationship because wrong customer assignments can still
sum to the same grand total.
Your independent practice
Merge accepted orders to M05_Customers.csv with validate="many_to_one" and
indicator=True. Reconcile rows/amount before and after. Then prove the duplicate-key
customer file fails the relationship contract.
Changed retry - only after review
Create a small product dimension with one duplicate key and prove a many-to-one merge guard
fails before aggregation; then repair the dimension and reconcile.
Ready-made revision
Reconstruct the core contract of pandas merge, cardinality and aggregation from memory.

Instructor / source: Corey Schafer - Python Pydantic Tutorial: Complete Data Validation
Course Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M81pfi64eeM Assigned use:
OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range; Pydantic context only.
Validation happens at more than one level. A record rule asks whether one row is acceptable:
does quantity parse and exceed zero? A batch rule asks about the set: are order IDs unique and
do accepted + rejected equal raw? A relationship rule crosses datasets: does every accepted
customer_id map to a declared customer, and is the dimension key unique? A robust pipeline
names all three instead of calling every check "validation."
Pydantic is useful because it can turn many type/field rules into explicit models and error
objects. But a Pydantic model is not a substitute for batch uniqueness, source-to-target
reconciliation or business relationships unless you build those checks too. Type hints and
successful model construction do not prove that a customer key exists in another file.
Use a small model only after you understand the manual rule. For example, parse quantity as a
positive integer and unit_price as a nonnegative decimal. Inspect the validation error rather
than catching every exception and replacing the row silently. Keep the original raw record or
source position next to the error evidence.
A critical distinction: technical validity and business validity differ. 2026-09-01 may parse as a
date, yet still be outside the allowed business period for a particular batch.
customer_id='C999' is a valid string but may violate referential integrity. 0 is a valid integer
but may violate a positive-quantity rule.
The changed retry asks you to add one syntactically valid record that fails only a relationship
rule. Your explanation should identify exactly which validation layer catches it and why
record-level parsing alone cannot.
Follow with me once
Separate validation by scope. A record rule can inspect one row; a batch rule needs the whole
collection; a relationship rule needs another entity or lookup.
from collections import Counter
rows = [
{"order_id":"A1", "customer_id":"C1", "qty":2},
{"order_id":"A1", "customer_id":"C2", "qty":1},
{"order_id":"A3", "customer_id":"C99", "qty":0},
valid_customers = {"C1", "C2"}
counts = Counter(r["order_id"] for r in rows)
for row in rows:
reasons = []
if row["qty"] <= 0:
reasons.append("qty_must_be_positive")              # record rule
if counts[row["order_id"]] > 1:
reasons.append("duplicate_order_id")                # batch rule
if row["customer_id"] not in valid_customers:
reasons.append("unknown_customer_id")               # relationship rule
print(row["order_id"], reasons)
A1 cannot be judged duplicate by looking at one record in isolation; that fact only exists at batch
scope. C99 may be syntactically valid text yet invalid against the relationship contract. Naming
the scope prevents you from cramming every rule into one giant row function and then
wondering why cross-record defects escape.
Your independent practice
Classify at least six checks as record, batch or relationship rules. Implement one typed/field
validation with Pydantic or a clear manual equivalent, then add one batch uniqueness and one
relationship check.
Changed retry - only after review
Add a syntactically valid customer_id that does not exist in the dimension. Show record
validation passes while relationship validation fails.
Ready-made revision
Reconstruct the core contract of Data validation: record, batch and relationship rules from
memory. State the input grain/state, one failure mode, one independent validation, and what
evidence you would keep. Then do one fresh 10-20 minute micro-task without video, review or
AI solving open.

Instructor / source: DataTalksClub - Docker for Data Engineering: Postgres, Docker Compose,
and Real-World Workflows Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lP8xXebHmuE Assigned
use:
OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range; API/Python context only.
Book + local simulator required.
HTTP is the transport contract behind many APIs. A client sends a request containing a method,
URL, headers and sometimes a body. The server sends a response containing a status code,
headers and bytes. REST is a design style layered on HTTP; you do not need to memorize
philosophy before learning safe client behavior.
Picture a courier. A 200 status says the transport request succeeded according to the server; it
does not prove the box contains the schema or number of records your pipeline expected. A 401
means authentication failed. A 404 means the resource was not found. A 429 means the client is
being rate limited. 5xx generally means the server encountered a failure. The exact handling
policy belongs to the API contract and operation.
Run M05_Local_API.py in one terminal. It binds only to 127.0.0.1 and provides /health,
authenticated /v1/orders, /v1/flaky, /v1/rate-limit and one deliberately non-JSON
endpoint. This makes failure practice repeatable even when internet access is unavailable.
For each endpoint, predict the status and content type before writing extraction logic. Do not
immediately call .json() on every 200 response. The simulator's /bad-content returns status
200 with text/plain specifically to prove that transport success is not payload validity.
Independent proof: build a tiny response-contract table with method, endpoint, authentication
requirement, acceptable statuses, expected media type and expected body shape. That table is
more valuable than memorizing requests.get() syntax.
Follow with me once
Treat HTTP as a request/response contract before worrying about Python syntax. Start the
supplied local API in one terminal:
python practice/M05_Local_API.py
Then in another terminal inspect the health endpoint:
import requests
r = requests.get("http://127.0.0.1:8765/health", timeout=5)
print("status=", r.status_code)
print("content_type=", r.headers.get("Content-Type"))
print("body=", r.json())
Expected status is 200 and JSON body is {"status": "ok"}. Now request a missing route and
observe 404. Request /v1/orders without the fictional training token and observe 401.
Those status codes are part of the contract. A server responding is not the same as a successful
business response. Your code should distinguish transport failure, HTTP failure, content-type
mismatch and valid JSON with unexpected fields. This mental model is what the later requests
helper will enforce.
Your independent practice
Run the local API and build a contract table for /health, /v1/orders, /bad-content, /v1/flaky and
/v1/rate-limit: auth, expected statuses, media type, body shape, retry policy.
Changed retry - only after review
Add a local endpoint/fixture expectation where status is 200 but required field is absent. Explain
why transport succeeded while contract validation failed.

Instructor / source: Requests Quickstart (official) Link:
https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/quickstart/ Assigned use: Timeouts,
errors/exceptions, response handling. Official current reference checked 14 Sep 2026.
The Requests library makes HTTP convenient, which means it can also make unsafe code look
deceptively simple. Production-style code should normally use an explicit timeout. The current
Requests documentation warns that without one, calls can wait indefinitely.
raise_for_status() converts unsuccessful HTTP statuses into exceptions, but you still need to
validate media type and payload shape after transport succeeds.
Use a sequence you can explain: construct URL/params and safe headers; send with timeout;
inspect status; raise for disallowed status; check expected content type; parse JSON; validate
required fields. Do not log an Authorization header while debugging. If a token appears in an
exception or URL, sanitize it before saving evidence.
Different failures deserve different names. A timeout is not the same as a 401; a 500 is not the
same as invalid JSON; a valid JSON error object is not the same as a valid order payload.
Catching Exception around the whole pipeline and printing "API failed" destroys information
you need to recover.
Use the local API client to fetch one page. Then intentionally call the non-JSON endpoint and
prove your media-type check fails before JSON decoding is trusted. Change the timeout to an
unrealistically small value only in a controlled test if you need to see timeout behavior; do not
make fragile timing tests part of mastery.
For the changed retry, call a missing endpoint. Your program should distinguish 404 from a
connection failure and should not retry it as though the server were temporarily overloaded.
Follow with me once
Use requests with three explicit safety checks: a timeout, HTTP-status handling, and
response-type validation.
import requests
url = "http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/orders?page=1&page_size=3"
headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer training-token"}  # fictional local token only
r = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=5)
r.raise_for_status()
ctype = r.headers.get("Content-Type", "").lower()
if "application/json" not in ctype:
raise ValueError(f"Expected JSON, got {ctype!r}")
payload = r.json()
print("records=", len(payload["records"]), "next_page=", payload["next_page"])
With page size 3, the first page should contain 3 records and next_page should be 2. Now call
/bad-content; it returns HTTP 200 but text/plain. This proves why status 200 alone is not
enough.
Never print a real Authorization header into logs or screenshots. The local training-token is
deliberately fictional so you can learn the pattern without creating a real secret.

Instructor / source: Using Python to consume an API with pagination - Renato Coelho Link:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vx6pmmRqCxI Assigned use: 04:50-13:40 - Coding API
pagination. Stop at the published Final explanation chapter boundary. Use the course local
API for authentication, completeness and failure evidence.
A paginated API can return a perfectly valid first page and still give you an incomplete dataset.
Pagination is therefore an integrity problem, not merely a loop exercise. The client must know
how the server signals the next page/cursor and must prove the stop condition was reached.
The local /v1/orders endpoint returns records, page, page_size, total and next_page. The
course client follows next_page until it becomes null. It also tracks seen order IDs. At the end,
compare fetched count, unique-key count and server-declared total. If those do not agree, do
not call the extraction complete.
Authentication is configuration, not code. Set M05_API_TOKEN=training-token only for this
fictional local simulator. In real projects, use the environment/secret mechanism approved by
the platform and never commit real tokens. Your logs may say auth configured: yes; they
should not print the secret value.
Pagination strategies vary: page numbers, offsets, next URLs and opaque cursors. Do not invent
the next value if the contract supplies one. A cursor can encode server state and may not be
mathematically incrementable. Also decide how a restart behaves: if page 3 fails after pages 1-2
were landed, can you safely replay them, or must you resume from persisted state?
Independent task: fetch all seven simulator orders with page_size=2, then again with
page_size=4. The same seven unique IDs and total amount must result. Explain why changing
page size should not change the logical dataset.

Instructor / source: Requests Quickstart (official) Link:
https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/quickstart/ Assigned use: Timeout/error
behavior, paired with the course fail-once/429 simulator and bounded retry policy.
Retries are controlled repetition after failures that may recover. They are not a universal cure.
Connection errors, timeouts, selected 5xx responses and 429 rate limits may be transient. A
deterministic 401 caused by a wrong token usually will not improve because you waited one
second. Blindly retrying every status wastes resources and can amplify damage.
Bound the number of attempts. For 5xx/transient network errors, an exponential policy
increases delay between attempts; jitter adds a small random component so many clients do
not retry in lockstep. For 429, respect Retry-After when the server supplies it. Keep tests fast:
the local simulator returns Retry-After=1 once, then succeeds.
Operation semantics matter. Retrying a GET is often safer than retrying a write whose first
outcome is unknown. If a POST created a payment but the response was lost, repeating it could
create two payments unless the API provides an idempotency mechanism. In M05 we focus on
read/extraction requests; later pipeline modules deepen state and replay safety.
Partial failure is the more important engineering lesson. Imagine pages 1 and 2 succeeded but
page 3 failed. If your program writes complete=true before page 3, the next system may
consume incomplete data as though it were complete. Persist success state only after the
durable output and its validation are complete.
Use /reset, then /v1/flaky: first call returns 500, the bounded client retries and the next
succeeds. Repeat with /v1/rate-limit. Then remove the token and prove 401 is surfaced
without a pointless retry loop. Save attempt count/status evidence, not the token.
Follow with me once
Retry only failures that have a reasonable chance of succeeding later, and keep the retry count
bounded.
The supplied client treats 429, selected 5xx responses, timeouts and connection errors as
transient. It does not retry ordinary 401, 403 or 404 responses as though persistence will fix a
bad credential or wrong route.
# after the local API is running and M05_API_TOKEN=training-token
from M05_API_Client import get_json
print(get_json("/reset"))
print(get_json("/v1/flaky", max_attempts=3))
print(get_json("/v1/rate-limit", max_attempts=3))
The flaky endpoint fails with 500 once, then succeeds on attempt 2. The rate-limit endpoint
returns 429 + Retry-After: 1 once, then succeeds on attempt 2. The client waits according to
the contract instead of hammering the service.
A retry policy must also preserve idempotency. Repeating a GET is usually safer than blindly
repeating a request that creates a new record. "Retry four times" is not a universal reliability
rule; it is a bounded response to a classified failure.

Instructor / source: SQLAlchemy Unified Tutorial - Engine and transactions (official) Link:
https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/tutorial/dbapi_transactions.html Assigned use:
Engine/Connection, transaction scope, text(), bound parameters. Current 2.0 docs checked 14
SQLAlchemy sits between Python and database drivers. An Engine describes how to obtain
connections; creating it does not necessarily establish a network connection immediately. A
Connection is a scoped database resource. Transactions decide whether a group of changes
commits together or rolls back when something fails.
Use your PostgreSQL environment from M03 for learner evidence when it is available. Put the
URL in M05_DATABASE_URL; do not write username/password directly into a committed .py file.
The bundled QA uses an isolated SQLite URL only to prove the SQLAlchemy code path without
pretending that SQLite execution proves PostgreSQL runtime behavior. Those are different
evidence levels.
The current SQLAlchemy 2.0 tutorial demonstrates two important habits: use a context manager
for connection scope, and use bound parameters rather than formatting untrusted values into
SQL strings. text("... WHERE amount >= :min_amount") plus a parameter dictionary lets
SQLAlchemy/driver handle the literal value safely.
For writes, with engine.begin() as conn: creates a transaction block that commits on
success and rolls back if an exception escapes. That is easier to reason about than a series of
untracked commits. For a pipeline load, decide which group of writes must be atomic. One giant
transaction is not always right, but accidental partial commits are worse.
Independent task: create a training table under your learner schema, insert two records with
bound parameters, read them back, and intentionally trigger a duplicate-key failure inside a
transaction. Prove whether the failed transaction left partial new data. Save your actual
PostgreSQL result if you ran PostgreSQL; label any SQLite fallback honestly.
Follow with me once
Keep connection configuration outside code and use an explicit transaction for writes.
import os
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text
url = os.environ["M05_DATABASE_URL"]
engine = create_engine(url)
with engine.begin() as conn:
conn.execute(text("""
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS m05_demo (
order_id VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
amount NUMERIC NOT NULL
conn.execute(
text("INSERT INTO m05_demo(order_id, amount) VALUES (:order_id, :amount)"),
[{"order_id":"DB01", "amount":1200}, {"order_id":"DB02", "amount":800}],
with engine.connect() as conn:
rows = conn.execute(
text("SELECT order_id, amount FROM m05_demo WHERE amount >= :minimum"),
{"minimum": 900},
).mappings().all()
print(rows)
The bound parameter :minimum is data, not SQL text concatenation. engine.begin() commits
the successful unit of work and rolls it back if an exception escapes the block.
For QA the package can use isolated SQLite to prove the Python/SQLAlchemy mechanics, but
your learner evidence should use the PostgreSQL environment established earlier. Do not
confuse a successful SQLite smoke test with proof that your PostgreSQL connection, permissions
and schema context are correct.

Instructor / source: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics Link:

environment/project setup context; secrets policy comes from this course.
Configuration answers "what changes between environments without editing program logic?" A
database URL, API base URL, input folder and log level are configuration. A real password/token
is a secret. Keeping both outside source code reduces accidental commits and makes the same
code usable on different machines.
Environment variables are one simple mechanism. Read them with os.getenv/os.environ and
validate required values near program startup. Failing early with M05_DATABASE_URL is
required is better than running half a pipeline and failing during the final load. Defaults are
appropriate only when the default is genuinely safe and unambiguous.
A .env file is a convenience used by some tools/libraries; Python does not automatically load it
by magic. If you use one later, keep .env out of version control and provide .env.example
containing variable names and fictional placeholders, never real credentials. M06 will make
.gitignore and repository hygiene explicit.
Do not log secrets. Also do not hide every configuration value: safe operational settings such as
batch date, input path, page size and log level can be valuable run metadata. Classify
configuration fields into safe-to-log versus sensitive and document the distinction.
The changed retry uses two configurations pointing to different local input folders. Without
changing the program body, prove the correct folder is selected and that a missing required
variable fails before any output files are written.

Instructor / source: PyCon US 2025 - Building Resilient Data Pipelines: The Power of
Idempotency Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kT8YWX4NE2o Assigned use:
OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range; idempotency/testing context only.
A pipeline needs observable behavior and tests that protect its contracts. Logging is structured
evidence about what the program did: run ID, source file, counts, durations, status and error
class. Logging started and finished alone does not prove correctness. Never include
tokens/passwords or unnecessarily dump personal/raw data into logs.
Use levels deliberately: DEBUG for detailed development diagnostics, INFO for normal lifecycle
milestones, WARNING for recoverable abnormal conditions, ERROR for failed operations. A
useful error message identifies the operation and safe context, while the exception/traceback
preserves technical detail. Do not catch an error only to replace it with a vague string.
Unit tests isolate small deterministic functions such as validate_orders. Integration tests
check boundaries between parts: reading a fixture, calling the local API, or writing/reading a
database. A test should assert an invariant, not merely that no exception occurred. The visible
tests prove a valid record computes amount correctly and a duplicated key is rejected.
Idempotency means repeating the same logical operation does not multiply the intended state.
The PyCon 2025 source is useful because it frames idempotency as a pipeline design criterion
and connects it to testing. In this module, your file-output checkpoint should overwrite or
atomically replace a declared run output rather than append accepted rows again on every
rerun. Later modules add more sophisticated checkpoints and incremental state.
Independent task: add one test for an invalid date and one for missing customer ID. Then run
the same reference pipeline twice and compare row counts/checksum or logical outputs. If the
second run doubles rows, the design is not safe to rerun.

Make the pipeline observable and testable without turning every function into a print statement.
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("m05")
def reconcile(raw_count, accepted_count, rejected_count):
if raw_count != accepted_count + rejected_count:
raise AssertionError("row reconciliation failed")
log.info(
"reconciled raw=%s accepted=%s rejected=%s",
raw_count, accepted_count, rejected_count,
reconcile(9, 4, 5)
A useful log states what happened without dumping confidential records or tokens. A useful
test asserts a behavior such as duplicate IDs being rejected. The supplied
M05_Visible_Tests.py contains one valid-record test and one duplicate-ID test; run it before
changing the validator, then add an edge case of your own.
Idempotency is a separate property: if you rerun the same valid input, the logical result should
not silently double. A deterministic overwrite of derived files can be idempotent; blind append
usually is not. Later orchestration modules will depend heavily on this habit.

The integrated pipeline combines the habits of the module into one defensible flow: identify
exact source -> preserve raw identity/checksum -> parse -> validate -> split accepted/rejected
-> transform accepted records -> optionally enrich/load -> reconcile -> save run metadata ->
prove rerun behavior. Each arrow is a contract boundary, not merely a function call.
Your module practical uses nine raw orders. Do not begin by reading the expected answer from
the review. Build from M05_Checkpoint_TODO.py in your own working folder. Save the first
attempt even if it fails. A good solution will surface the invalid records with reasons rather than
editing them away; preserve source row numbers or equivalent provenance so a reviewer can
trace each rejection.
The core reconciliation is multidimensional. Raw row count must equal accepted plus rejected.
Accepted order IDs must be unique. Every rejected row must have a reason. Accepted amount
must equal the independent sum of accepted quantity x price. Source checksum/run metadata
must point to the exact input. If you enrich with customers, merge cardinality must not change
accepted order grain or amount.
Then deliberately create a failure. Use the duplicate-customer file with a many-to-one merge
assertion, or replace the expected order schema with a malformed file. The pipeline should stop
at the first violated contract and should not publish a misleading "successful" final artifact. Keep
the failed evidence before repairing it.
Finally rerun the same exact source. The logical output should not grow simply because the
command was executed twice. After review, close the answer book and solve the fresh
inventory checkpoint with different columns, identifiers, validation rules and total. That fresh
transfer is the real mastery evidence for M05.
